article.content_html:
Key Developments

  • The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) confirmed the arrests of at least 40 ultra-Orthodox men at Ben Gurion Airport.
  • The individuals were detained upon arrival, suspected of attempting to evade mandatory military service, and will be tried in accordance with the law.
  • The IDF described the mass arrest as unusual in its scale, highlighting the growing tension around the issue of military service.
  • Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose government relies on ultra-Orthodox party support, publicly opposed the arrests in an interview with ultra-Orthodox radio station Kol Barama, arguing they harm efforts to enlist them without coercion.

Key Takeaways

  • The arrests of ultra-Orthodox men for draft evasion mark a significant escalation in Israel's long-standing debate over military service exemptions.
  • The issue has gained urgency following the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks and subsequent multi-front war, fueling calls for equality of service among all Israeli citizens.
  • Prime Minister Netanyahu faces a delicate political balancing act, needing ultra-Orthodox support while also addressing public demands for broader conscription.

Why It Matters

For decades, ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) Jews have largely been exempt from military service, with most men studying full-time in religious seminaries. However, in 2024, Israel's Supreme Court ruled that in the absence of any law legalizing this exemption, the military must begin drafting them.

The demographic reality further complicates the issue: ultra-Orthodox Jews constitute about 13% of Israel's population, a figure projected to reach nearly 25% by 2050. This rapid growth makes their non-participation a growing burden on the military and society, as many Israelis who serve, particularly in the reserves, complain of having to take on an unfair amount of the security burden.

Ultra-Orthodox political leaders are pushing for a new law to formalize broad exemptions while also setting a percentage of ultra-Orthodox men and women who would be subject to compulsory service. With national elections looming on October 27, this issue has become a central point of political contention, directly impacting Prime Minister Netanyahu's ability to maintain his coalition, as he has relied on ultra-Orthodox parties since the 2022 elections.
